title: Given Only an Afternoon to Code, Submitting a PPT Wins Instead: AI Hackathons Are Losing Their Way

content_html:
In June 1999, the OpenBSD community held the world's first hackathon, where developers spent a week integrating the IPv6 protocol stack into the system. But according to a November 23 report by Chaoping, today there are hundreds of AI hackathons a year in China, yet the development time has been compressed to a single afternoon. Many people can't produce deliverables, and can even win awards with just a concept PPT—participants bluntly say this is more like a "PPT creativity contest."

Contestants Network, Investors Freeload

After talking with multiple contestants and organizers, a mismatched picture emerges: some treat the competition as a social platform, bringing finished products to pitch for investment, and can take the same project around to various events and win awards repeatedly—organizers don't stop them, since mature projects present better. Investors' calculation is to scout people and freeload: projects are mostly generated from a few rounds of prompts, with almost no moat; handing over a project proposal may get your ideas taken and your people poached. As for judging, time is short and judges are unprofessional, so the key to winning becomes whether it looks good and whether the pitch has stage presence. Project homogenization is also severe; ideas like Pomodoro timers can be seen at every event—one author in 2025 pitched "Am I Dead?" with a PPT, but the product was never actually built; the app that later became popular was someone else's.

Thousand-Person Events Are Chaotic, Half-Month Residencies Are Better
